opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to a few things converging at once. The first is just that the models got good enough at reasoning over long horizons. A year or two ago, if you asked a model to go off and do a multi-step task, search, read a bunch of documents, synthesize, check its own work, it would drift. It would lose the thread, hallucinate a citation, or just stop early. That reliability has improved a lot, and research is a task where you can tolerate the model taking a few minutes, or even longer, as long as what comes back is genuinely good.

The second thing is that the shape of the task fits the technology really well. Research is fundamentally about gathering information from lots of sources, cross-referencing it, and producing a grounded summary with evidence. That plays directly to what these systems are strong at: reading enormous amounts of text far faster than any human could, and doing it with citations so you can verify the output. The verification piece is critical. In enterprise settings, people don't want a black box answer; they want to see where it came from. Deep research gives you that audit trail naturally.

And third, the value is really obvious to the buyer. When you talk to analysts at a bank, or people in legal, or consultants, a huge chunk of their week is spent doing exactly this kind of desk research. If you can compress something that took two days into twenty minutes, and the quality is comparable to what a solid junior analyst would produce, that's an easy ROI conversation. You don't have to convince anyone it's useful.

The caveat I'd add is that the real unlock in enterprise is connecting it to private data. Searching the public web is great, but most of the value inside a company lives in internal documents, emails, databases, CRMs. So the version of deep research that really transforms work is the one that can securely reason over a company's own knowledge alongside the outside world. That's where we've been spending a lot of our energy, and I think that's where you'll see the biggest impact over the next year or two.

r001.rationale: The response says deep research could compress work that took two days into twenty minutes; it does not state that a report taking roughly a month and a half for a human can be produced.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that deep research is one of the first places where the technology and the actual job finally line up. For a long time we were trying to force models into tasks they weren't quite good enough for, and users could feel the gap. Research is different. The task is: go read a lot of stuff, pull out what matters, cross-reference it, and come back with something structured. That's exactly what these models are now genuinely good at.

A few things came together to make it work. The first is retrieval and tool use maturing. The model isn't guessing from its weights anymore, it's going out, pulling documents, reading them, and citing them. That changes the trust equation completely. If I can click through and check the source, I can actually use the output in my work, rather than treating it as a curiosity.

The second is that the models got much better at operating over long horizons. Deep research isn't one prompt, one answer. It's dozens of steps, each one depending on the last. A year or two ago the error rate per step compounded and you'd end up somewhere nonsensical. Now the models can plan, notice when a thread is a dead end, and recover. That reliability threshold is what makes it a product rather than a demo.

And the third piece is just the economics. The people who do this work professionally, analysts, consultants, lawyers, researchers inside enterprises, they are expensive and they spend an enormous fraction of their time on the gathering and synthesis part, not the judgment part. If you can compress a two-day literature review into twenty minutes, nobody needs convincing on the ROI. It's one of the rare cases where the value is obvious to the buyer without any education.

What I'd say to be careful about is that the latency and cost are real. People are willing to wait ten or fifteen minutes for a good answer, but only when the stakes justify it. So I don't think it's a replacement for the quick chat interaction, it's a different mode. But for the high-stakes, high-effort question, it's ready, and I think it's where a lot of the real enterprise value gets unlocked over the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says a two-day literature review could be compressed into twenty minutes. It does not state that the AI can produce a report that would take a human roughly a month and a half.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re ready because the task is valuable, and you can give the model time to do it well. If I ask a complicated research question, I don’t necessarily need an answer in half a second. I’d rather it spend a few minutes searching, comparing sources, and putting together something I can actually use.

That’s also a workflow where the human can review the result. You can look at the sources, check whether the evidence supports the conclusions, and decide where to dig further. It doesn’t have to autonomously make the final decision to save you a lot of work.

So you have this combination of a useful task, room to spend more time on the answer, and an output that someone can inspect. That makes it a pretty compelling place to put these capabilities into people’s hands.

r001.rationale: The response says deep research can take a few minutes and save work, but does not state that its report could replace roughly a month and a half of human preparation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you can give the model a task that’s worth spending real time on. You’re not asking for an instant answer; you’re asking it to go away, investigate something, and come back with a useful report. That gives it room to search, compare sources, and check its work.

And the output is something you can review. You can look at the evidence, follow the citations, and decide whether the conclusion makes sense. It doesn’t have to autonomously run your business to be valuable. If it gets you to a solid first draft of research that would otherwise take hours, that’s already a pretty compelling product.

r001.rationale: The response says the research could save hours and produce a useful report, but does not state that it could take a human roughly a month and a half to prepare.
